strengths: The paper addresses an important and persistent weakness of text-to-image diffusion models: count failures and semantic leakage in multi-object, especially intra-category, scenes. The instance-first framing is well motivated by the attention visualizations and by the distinction between self-attention structure and cross-attention semantics.

ISAC is technically simple, training-free, and broadly applicable to several diffusion backbones. The two-phase objective, first clustering self-attention into instance masks and then using those masks for semantic repel/bind losses, is a plausible and useful extension of prior attention-control methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad: results are reported on HRS-Bench, T2I-CompBench, the proposed IntraCompBench, multiple Stable Diffusion/PixArt/SD3.5/Flux/Qwen-style backbones, count-supervised baselines, layout-to-image control with GLIGEN, ablations on schedule/metric/clustering, and appendix analyses of stability and quality trade-offs.

The gains on the proposed intra-category setting are substantial, especially for crowded multi-class prompts where prior attention-control methods remain weak. The ablations support the main design claim that instance formation before semantic separation is preferable to semantic-only or reversed schedules.
The paper is generally clear and well organized, with helpful qualitative figures, algorithmic description, implementation details, and a stated limitation regarding 3D/spatial reasoning.
weaknesses: The main practical drawback is cost. ISAC roughly doubles or triples latency on smaller models and is very expensive on larger backbones, with SD3.5-M requiring around 140s and about 75GB VRAM for latent optimization. This limits real-world usability, and the more efficient latent-selection variant is only evaluated as an appendix alternative rather than integrated into the main comparison.

The benchmark and evaluation protocol rely heavily on detector ensembles over COCO-style countable classes. This makes the evaluation reproducible in principle, but it risks measuring detector-friendliness rather than human-perceived compositional correctness, excludes many realistic object categories, and may not fully capture over-generation, spatial plausibility, or attribute binding errors. A human evaluation or stronger validation of the detector-based metric would make the empirical case more convincing.

The method requires prompt parsing into counts, class tokens, and token relations using an LLM parser. This is a nontrivial dependency, reportedly requiring substantial VRAM, and ambiguous count expressions are not handled. This somewhat weakens the claim of broad model-agnostic, training-free deployment, since inference depends on reliable structured prompt extraction.

Novelty is moderate rather than overwhelming. The method combines known ingredients from prior work: attention hooks, latent optimization, self-attention structural cues, cross-attention semantic maps, repel/bind objectives, and clustering. The contribution is mainly the effective instance-to-semantic organization and loss schedule, which is valuable but not a fundamentally new generative model or theory.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. For example, 'applicable to any diffusion models' assumes access to internal attention maps and manageable gradient memory, and layout-to-image evidence is limited to GLIGEN/HRS-Bench while OverLayBench is deferred. The paper would benefit from more careful qualification of these boundaries.

Image quality/aesthetic impact is only lightly quantified. The appendix reports FID/CMMD relative to SDXL outputs on one numeracy setting, but the large guidance changes and detector-optimized objectives could produce artifacts or unnatural scenes that are not fully reflected in the presented metrics.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated failure mode in text-to-image generation: multi-instance counting and semantic leakage among similar objects. The instance-first framing is intuitive and relevant to current controllable generation problems.
The method is training-free and, in principle, applicable to several diffusion backbones because it operates through internal self- and cross-attention maps rather than requiring model retraining.

The empirical section is broad: results are reported on HRS-Bench, T2I-CompBench, the proposed IntraCompBench, multiple backbones, layout-to-image generation, ablations of the loss schedule, similarity metric, clustering method, and some efficiency measurements.

The ablations in Tables 5 and 6 support the central design choices: separating instance formation from semantic assignment and using the proposed MPO overlap objective both appear beneficial on the authors' benchmark.

The paper is generally readable and includes useful implementation details in the appendix, including prompt parsing instructions, class lists, detector ensemble evaluation, and limitations around 3D reasoning.
weaknesses: The core technical novelty is limited. The method combines known ingredients: attention-map extraction, self-attention clustering, latent optimization, token relation parsing, and cross-attention separation/binding losses. The paper presents this as a new hierarchy, but the algorithmic advance over prior attention-control and self/cross-attention guidance methods is incremental.

The main benchmark, IntraCompBench, is not fully convincing as evidence for the strong claims. Evaluation is based on open-vocabulary/object detectors over COCO-like classes, and the appendix defines accuracy as detected requested instances divided by target instances rather than strict prompt success. This weakens claims about exact instance formation, count correctness, and semantic assignment.

The evaluation may be biased toward detector-friendly COCO categories and does not include human evaluation or a strong VLM-based sanity check. Since the task is visual compositional correctness, detector failure modes and false positives/negatives could substantially affect the reported gains.

The method requires parsed instance counts and token relations at inference time, using a 20B LLM parser that itself takes around 10 seconds and 40GB VRAM for moderately complex prompts. This dependency is underemphasized in the main efficiency comparisons and complicates the claim of being lightweight or broadly model-agnostic.

The computational overhead is substantial: latent optimization roughly doubles or triples memory and latency, with SD3.5-M requiring around 75GB VRAM for guided methods and SDXL ISAC reaching around 100s latency. The latent-selection alternative is discussed, but it is a different best-of-N sampling regime and not directly comparable to the main method.

Several claims are overstated. For example, 'applicable to any diffusion models' is too broad because the method needs accessible attention maps and model internals; 'surpassing count-supervised methods' is shown mainly on the authors' benchmark and may not establish general superiority.

Comparison fairness is not entirely clear. Baselines may not receive the same structured prompt parsing, count information, or optimization budget, and the paper does not sufficiently separate the contribution of the parser/count supervision from the attention-control objective.

The proposed benchmark is useful but narrow: it excludes difficult or ambiguous classes, focuses on COCO categories, and samples only a subset of combinations. This is reasonable for automatic evaluation, but the paper's conclusions about robust multi-object generation go beyond what this setup establishes.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time because code is only promised upon publication. Given the many implementation choices in attention aggregation, normalization, clustering, parsing, and detector-based scoring, public code is important for verifying the results.

The limitation discussion is too narrow. It mentions 3D/transparent-object failures, but more central limitations include detector-based evaluation reliability, parser ambiguity, high compute cost, dependence on explicit counts, and potential degradation of aesthetics or natural layouts under strong latent optimization.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practical failure mode in text-to-image generation: multi-instance count errors and semantic leakage among similar objects. The instance-first framing is well motivated by attention visualizations and connects clearly to the proposed method.

ISAC is a technically sensible training-free contribution: clustering self-attention to form instance layouts, then using instance-aware semantic masks for repel/bind guidance is a coherent design that differs meaningfully from prior cross-attention-only guidance methods.

The empirical evidence is broad. Results cover SD1.x, SDXL, SD3.5, PixArt, Flux/Qwen via latent selection, public compositional benchmarks, the proposed IntraCompBench, layout-to-image control, count-supervised comparisons, and fine-tuned model integration.

The ablations are useful and support the core claims: the instance-to-semantic schedule outperforms reversed/fixed schedules, MPO is better than alternative overlap metrics, and clustering choices and step-size sensitivity are discussed.
The new IntraCompBench targets a real evaluation gap: intra-category multi-object composition is harder than standard compositional benchmarks and is directly aligned with the claimed contribution.
The manuscript is generally clear, with detailed appendices covering parsing prompts, evaluation protocol, efficiency, latent selection, limitations, and additional qualitative results.
weaknesses: The method depends on knowing or extracting instance counts and object/attribute relations at inference time. This is reasonable for the claimed setting, but limits the strength of the “model-agnostic” and general-purpose framing, especially for ambiguous natural prompts such as plurals, “several,” or complex relational descriptions.

Evaluation on the new benchmark relies heavily on open-vocabulary/object detectors and COCO-derived classes. This makes the reported accuracies partly dependent on detector behavior and narrows evidence for generalization beyond countable, detector-friendly categories.

The computational overhead is substantial. Latent optimization roughly doubles or triples memory and latency for several backbones, and the LLM parser itself is reported to require about 40 GB VRAM for some prompts. The latent-selection variant helps, but changes the trade-off to best-of-N sampling rather than direct guidance.

Some headline gains remain modest in the hardest cases: for example, multi-class #5 accuracy is still low in absolute terms even after ISAC, suggesting the approach improves but does not solve crowded compositional generation.

The layout-to-image evaluation avoids OverLayBench due to prompt-format incompatibility. The explanation is plausible, but it leaves the strongest overlapping-layout benchmark largely untested despite overlap handling being one of the paper’s stated extensions.

Image quality is only lightly quantified. FID/CMMD are measured relative to the base model distribution on a limited setting, and the method’s tendency to alter aesthetics or introduce artifacts would benefit from stronger human or preference-model evaluation.

Reproducibility is good in description but not complete at submission time: code is promised after publication, and the method has many implementation-sensitive components such as attention extraction, normalization, clustering, parser outputs, and detector-based evaluation.
